lead: An analog cockpit gives every quantity its own dial, driven by its own sensor. A glass cockpit draws the same quantities on a few screens, from computers that read the sensors over data buses. Glass saves panel space, weight and crew workload and can show pictures no dial can, such as a moving map. In exchange it depends on electrical power, cooling and software, so a glass cockpit is designed around what happens when a screen, a computer or the power fails.
prereq: You need: Avionics system architecture, IMA and LRUs for how sensors and computers are connected.

sections.h3: The analog cockpit: one dial per job

blocks.text: The flight instruments of an analog cockpit are the basic six, set out in the basic T: the attitude indicator at the top centre, the airspeed indicator to its left, the altimeter to its right, and the heading indicator below the attitude indicator. The turn coordinator and the vertical speed indicator fill the two lower corners. Three are pitot-static instruments (airspeed, altitude, vertical speed) and three are gyroscopic (attitude, heading, turn). Engine dials sit beside them: tachometer, exhaust gas temperature, oil pressure and temperature, fuel quantity. How these instruments work is covered in Air data instruments and Engine instruments: tachometer and EGT.

items: Each dial shows one quantity and has its own case, lighting and wiring.
A failed dial blanks only its own quantity, and a pneumatic or vacuum dial still works after an electrical failure.
The pilot must scan a wide panel and combine the readings in the head.
Every new function means another instrument and more panel space.

blocks.text: Examples: the Cessna 172 with its six-pack, the Boeing 727 and the early Boeing 747, where a flight engineer watched a separate panel of system dials.

sections.h3: The glass cockpit: screens, symbol generators and pages

blocks.text: An electronic flight instrument system (EFIS) has three parts: display units (the screens), display computers or symbol generators that turn sensor data into pictures, and control panels on which the crew selects modes and ranges. Early screens were colour cathode-ray tubes (CRTs); modern ones are active-matrix liquid-crystal displays (LCDs), which are lighter, cooler and readable in sunlight. Data arrives on buses from the air data and inertial units, the flight management system and the engine computers.

A page is a screen layout. One screen can show the primary flight page, a navigation map, an engine page or a system synoptic, chosen by the crew or brought up automatically when a fault appears. Because the drawing is software, one screen replaces several dials and the same screens can show weather radar, traffic and terrain.

blocks.text: A hybrid cockpit keeps some dials and adds screens; it was the normal step in the 1980s and is still a common upgrade. The engine and alerting screens of the 757, 767 and A310 also let a two-person crew do the job of the flight engineer.

A dial needs a sensor and a wire. A glass picture needs a sensor, a bus, a display computer, a screen, electrical power and cooling. Each link can fail, and one failed computer or power bus can blank several screens at once. Glass cockpits answer this in three ways.

items: Reversion: if a screen fails, its page moves to another screen, automatically or by a switch. On many airliners the primary flight page moves to the navigation screen next to it.
Standby instruments: a small standby display (or standby dials) with its own sensors and its own battery shows attitude, airspeed and altitude when everything else is lost.

Load shedding: on battery power the electrical system switches off everything except the essential screens and sensors, so the battery lasts long enough to land (see Emergency power: ram air turbine and ETOPS).

blocks.text: Software defects and bad data are the other risk: a screen can show a confident-looking wrong value. So each value carries a validity status, and invalid data is replaced by a failure flag instead of being drawn (see Electronic displays).

examples.question: A light aircraft has a glass cockpit and a 24 V, 10 Ah battery of which 80 % can be used. With the alternator failed, the loads are: primary display 60 W, multifunction display 60 W, attitude and air data unit 20 W, standby display 15 W and radios 40 W. (a) Find the usable battery energy. (b) Find the battery time with all loads on. (c) The pilot sheds the multifunction display and the radios. Find the new battery time.
steps: Battery energy: 24 V × 10 Ah = 240 Wh. Usable: 0.80 × 240 = 192 Wh.
Time with all loads: 192 Wh ÷ 195 W = 0.985 h = 0.985 × 60 = 59 minutes.
Time after shedding: 192 Wh ÷ 95 W = 2.02 h = 121 minutes.
Check: 95 W × 2.02 h = 192 Wh, the usable energy.
examples.answer: Usable energy 192 Wh; about 59 minutes with every load on, and about 121 minutes (2.0 h) after shedding the multifunction display and radios. Load shedding doubles the time available to reach an airfield.

traps: Writing that a glass cockpit removes sensors. The pitot-static system, gyros or inertial sensors and engine sensors are all still there; only the indicator changed.
Calling a hybrid cockpit a failed upgrade. It is a deliberate mix of dials and screens.
Forgetting the standby instruments in a glass cockpit answer. Examiners expect them with their own battery.
Comparing only normal operation. Compare failure modes: one dial lost versus one screen or one power bus lost.
Using 24 V × 10 Ah = 240 W. Volts times ampere-hours gives watt-hours, energy, not power.

quiz.q: Name the basic six instruments and say which are pitot-static.
quiz.a: Airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter, turn coordinator, heading indicator, vertical speed indicator. The airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator are pitot-static.

quiz.q: Name the three parts of an EFIS.
quiz.a: Display units, display computers (symbol generators) and control panels.

quiz.q: Why did screens let airliners drop the flight engineer?
quiz.a: The engine and alerting screens watch the systems, show only what is abnormal and give the checklist, so the two pilots can manage the systems that a flight engineer used to monitor.

quiz.q: Why are LCDs preferred to CRTs in modern cockpits?
quiz.a: They are lighter, thinner, cooler and draw less power, and they stay readable in direct sunlight.

quiz.q: A 28 V, 12 Ah battery is 75 % usable. Essential loads are 120 W. Find the battery time in minutes.
quiz.a: Energy 28 × 12 = 336 Wh; usable 252 Wh. Time 252 ÷ 120 = 2.1 h = 126 minutes.

quiz.q: Compare the loss of one dial in an analog cockpit with the loss of one display computer in a glass cockpit.
quiz.a: One dial loses one quantity. One display computer can blank every screen it drives, so the design needs a second computer, reversion switching and standby instruments.

quiz.q: A pilot says glass is safer because screens never wear out. Evaluate the claim.
quiz.a: Screens have no moving parts and are more reliable than gyro dials, but the picture also depends on power, cooling, computers and software. Safety comes from redundancy, reversion, validity flags and standby instruments, not from the screen alone.

beyond: Not for the exam. New flight decks use large touchscreens that merge the primary, map and engine pages, and synthetic vision draws terrain from a database behind the attitude picture. Retrofit kits now turn analog light aircraft into glass cockpits with standby displays that carry their own battery. Search for 'synthetic vision', 'integrated standby instrument' and 'touchscreen flight deck'.
